title: Fugue in A minor
blurb: Four countersubject statements inside twenty-eight bars, and not one stretto.
card: The only fugue here whose key never officially changes: 28 bars, all of them A minor.
history: The subject takes a bar and three quarters to say eight notes, which leaves the semiquavers to the lines underneath and above it. Four of those lines recur often enough to count as countersubjects, so the company the subject keeps is steadier than the subject itself: only four of the eight entries come back exact. The eight are spread evenly through the 28 bars, none of them overlapping, and no episode reaches three bars.

The key analysis returns one region: A minor, bar 1 to bar 28. Nothing else on this site does that. Part of it is the tool being coarse — there are entries on G and on B, so the music is plainly going somewhere — but most of it is the piece. The chromaticism is local, the cadences keep landing back on A, and 28 bars is not long enough to properly leave.

Book II was put together in Leipzig around 1739–42, nearly twenty years after Book I, out of pieces Bach had been writing over a much longer span. The main source is the London autograph in the British Library, some of it in his hand, some in Anna Magdalena's.
